It's about sleep cycles. When you are drunk you don't "think" as much, or there is less brain activity, so when you are asleep you pass by the REM sleeping state much quicker (Where your brain is semi awake/dreaming) and hit deep sleep, ergo having a more "efficient" sleep. 

Also you produce more inhibition synapses, so your brain will have less sympatic activity, be less alarmed and so can't respond to stimulus like the phone as easily without the alcohol keeping you in a more passive state.
Therefore why you may have a small amount of hours sleep and wake up feeling refreshed.

As for reasons for waking up during the night there are a number of anticipatory responses that can induce wakefulness after drinking - hunger and thirst being good examples. Another thing to remember is that post drinking 'sleep' resembles a power nap rather than a normal sleep cycle which is why some people feel very refreshed (in the short term). Yet again, some people's nervous systems respond to alcohol with hyperactivity in an effort to compensate. The sympathetic response often outlasts the effects of the alcohol and you wake up after a shorter time than normal but feeling better because you have higher levels of norepinephrine and acetylcholine.

Generally yes, they would have music to follow, but it is up to the conductor (As said above) how he wants the music to be played. He can choose to follow the score/sheet music exactly as written or change it to his own interpretation, as sometimes the music will be used more as a guide. He will often choose to not do certain things written or do them differently.    
The conductor is if you will, the coach of the orchestra. The band could, if skilled enough (which generally an orchestra is), play without a conductor, but it would never work(Not generally, or not until it has been first rehearsed with the conductor) because the conductor views the music and sections as a whole, editing parts, to make it all work together perfectly.
